warmup.q: What does adding suspend to a function do?
options: It runs the function on a background thread
It lets the function pause at suspending calls and continue later, without holding a thread while it waits
It makes the function return a CompletableFuture
It runs the function in parallel with its caller
warmup.why: suspend only gives a function the ability to pause. It does not pick a thread, start anything in parallel or return a future. The thread is chosen by the coroutine's dispatcher, and a suspend function that never reaches a suspending call runs start to finish on its caller's thread.

sections.h: A suspend function can pause without blocking its thread
sections.html:
Most payment code has the same shape: call the card issuer and wait 120 ms, call the ledger and wait 30 ms, return. Nearly all of the time is waiting. With one thread per request, each thread spends that time parked and still holds its stack. The Kotlin docs put the cost plainly: a thread usually needs a few megabytes of memory, and a JVM typically handles a few thousand of them at once.

A suspend function is a function that can pause in the middle and continue later, without holding a thread while it is paused.

Java
// Java equivalent: plain blocking calls on a virtual thread (JDK 21+); the JVM does the pausing
Authorization charge(ChargeRequest req) {
    String token = vault.tokenize(req.pan());          // the virtual thread unmounts while it waits
    return issuer.authorize(token, req.amount());      // and here
}
Kotlin
suspend fun charge(req: ChargeRequest): Authorization {
    val token = vault.tokenize(req.pan)          // may pause here
    return issuer.authorize(token, req.amount)   // and here
}

When charge pauses inside tokenize, the thread leaves and runs other work. When the vault answers, charge continues on the next line, possibly on a different thread. The code still reads top to bottom, with normal try/catch and normal return values.

A coroutine is one running instance of such code: a piece of work that can be paused and resumed. You start one with a builder like runBlocking or launch (lesson 2 of this track). Two rules follow.

You can call a suspend function only from another suspend function or from inside a coroutine. Plain code has nothing to resume, so the compiler refuses.

Waiting must be done with a suspending call. delay(200) suspends: the coroutine is set aside and the thread is free. Thread.sleep(200) blocks: the thread stops, and every other coroutine that needs that thread waits too. The compiler accepts both, so nothing warns you.

The Try it runs five coroutines on a single thread, main. Each waits 200 ms. With delay, the five waits overlap. With Thread.sleep, the one thread can only sleep for one of them at a time.

try.title: Five waits on one thread
steps: Read SleepVsDelay.kt. All five coroutines run on main. Predict the total time with delay.
Run it with the command below.
Run it again with -Pargs=sleep added. Predict first, then watch how the five lines appear.

code.title: SleepVsDelay.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Five coroutines share ONE thread and each waits 200 ms. Pass "sleep" to block instead of suspend. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val blocking = args.firstOrNull() == "sleep" val took = measureTimeMillis { runBlocking { // runs every coroutine below on the main thread repeat(5) { i -> launch { println("payment $i starts waiting on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") if (blocking) Thread.sleep(200) else delay(200) } } } } val how = if (blocking) "Thread.sleep" else "delay" println("5 waits of 200 ms with $how took $took ms") }

alt.title: SleepVsDelayJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SleepVsDelay.kt: one thread, five 200 ms waits. // A non-blocking timer callback plays the role of delay; Thread.sleep blocks the one thread. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SleepVsDelayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { boolean blocking = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("sleep"); ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "main-loop")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> waits = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { int id = i; CompletableFuture<Void> done = new CompletableFuture<>(); oneThread.execute(() -> { System.out.println("payment " + id + " starts waiting on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); if (blocking) { sleep(200); // holds the only thread done.complete(null); } else { // a timer completes it later; the thread is free meanwhile CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, oneThread).execute(() -> done.complete(null)); } }); waits.add(done); } CompletableFuture.allOf(waits.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); String how = blocking ? "Thread.sleep" : "a timer callback"; System.out.printf("5 waits of 200 ms with %s took %d ms%n", how, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } private static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

try.expect: With delay the run takes a little over 200 ms (278 ms here): the waits overlap on one thread. With Thread.sleep it takes over a second (1,078 ms here), and the five lines appear 200 ms apart, because each sleep holds the only thread. Same code, one word changed. The Java twin gives the same two numbers (225 ms and 1,025 ms here): a timer callback on a single-thread executor is the closest Java match for delay.

sections.h: A suspend function runs on whatever thread calls it
sections.html:
The most common wrong idea about coroutines is that suspend sends work to a background thread. It does not. The modifier adds the ability to pause and nothing else. Which thread runs the code is decided by the coroutine's dispatcher, a scheduler you will meet in lesson 4 of this track.

Java
// Java equivalent: the same plain method; in Kotlin the suspend modifier changed nothing
int checksum(String digits) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (char c : digits.toCharArray()) sum = (sum * 31 + c) % 1_000_003;
    return sum;
}
Kotlin
suspend fun checksum(digits: String): Int {
    var sum = 0
    for (c in digits) sum = (sum * 31 + c.code) % 1_000_003
    return sum   // no suspension point anywhere
}

This function never suspends, so it runs start to finish on the caller's thread, exactly like a normal function. IntelliJ flags the modifier as redundant. Put a two-second CPU loop in a suspend function, call it from a request coroutine, and that request's thread is busy for two seconds. Marking it suspend changed nothing.

The other half of the story: after a real suspension, the coroutine may continue on a different thread. A coroutine on Dispatchers.Default can start on worker-1, pause in delay, and resume on worker-3. Two things follow for your code.

A ThreadLocal is not safe across a suspension point. The thread that resumes you may hold someone else's value. Logging MDC is a ThreadLocal, so this bites in real services. Lesson 4 of this track shows context elements, the coroutine way to carry such values.

Memory visibility, on the other hand, is handled for you. Values a coroutine wrote before it suspended are visible after it resumes, even on another thread. You don't need @Volatile on locals that live across a delay.

try.title: Watch coroutines change threads
steps: Read WhichThread.kt. Predict which thread computes the checksum.
Run it. Look at the payment N ran on lines.
Run it twice more. Do the thread sequences repeat?

code.title: WhichThread.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private fun where() = Thread.currentThread().name.removePrefix("DefaultDispatcher-") /** A suspend function that never suspends runs on its caller's thread, start to finish. */ suspend fun checksum(digits: String): Int { var sum = 0 for (c in digits) sum = (sum * 31 + c.code) % 1_000_003 return sum // no suspension point anywhere: plain code with a suspend label on it } fun main() = runBlocking { println("main coroutine runs on ${where()}") println("checksum ${checksum("4242424242424242")} computed on ${where()}") repeat(4) { id -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { val seen = mutableListOf<String>() repeat(4) { seen += where() delay(20) // suspends; any free Default thread may resume it } println("payment $id ran on ${seen.joinToString(" -> ")}") } } }

alt.title: WhichThreadJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of WhichThread.kt: virtual threads also move between carrier threads. // A plain method runs on its caller's thread; a virtual thread that sleeps may wake up on another carrier. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class WhichThreadJava { static int checksum(String digits) { // the same code as the Kotlin suspend fun: it never pauses int sum = 0; for (char c : digits.toCharArray()) sum = (sum * 31 + c) % 1_000_003; return sum; } // a virtual thread prints as VirtualThread[#29]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3; keep the carrier part static String carrier() { String s = Thread.currentThread().toString(); int at = s.indexOf('@'); return at < 0 ? Thread.currentThread().getName() : s.substring(at + 1).replace("ForkJoinPool-1-", ""); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("main runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); System.out.println("checksum " + checksum("4242424242424242") + " computed on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); List<Thread> payments = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = 0; id < 4; id++) { int pid = id; payments.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); for (int step = 0; step < 4; step++) { seen.add(carrier()); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // unmounts; any carrier may resume it } System.out.println("payment " + pid + " ran on " + String.join(" -> ", seen)); })); } for (Thread t : payments) t.join(); } }

try.expect: The checksum runs on main, the caller's thread. Each payment coroutine shows a sequence like worker-1 -> worker-1 -> worker-4 -> worker-3: after each delay any free Default worker may pick it up. The sequences change from run to run. The Java twin shows the same thing for virtual threads: after each Thread.sleep a virtual thread may continue on a different carrier.

sections.h: The compiler turns a suspend function into a state machine
sections.html:
Coroutines need no special support from the JVM. They are a compiler feature plus a library. The Kotlin compiler rewrites every suspend function in continuation-passing style: it adds one hidden last parameter, a Continuation, and changes the return type to Any?.

// you write
suspend fun chargeCard(pan: String): String

// javap shows
public static final java.lang.Object chargeCard(java.lang.String, kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<? super java.lang.String>);

A Continuation is a callback that also carries the coroutine's context: interface Continuation<in T> { val context: CoroutineContext; fun resumeWith(result: Result<T>) }. The Object return is either the real result or a marker, COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, which means "I paused; I will call your continuation later".

The body becomes a state machine. Each suspension point ends a state. The compiler generates one small class per suspend function (here StateMachineKt$chargeCard$1) with an int label for the next state and fields L$0, L$1 for locals that must survive a pause. Here is chargeCard from the demo, step by step:

  1. Label 0: store pan in the object, set label = 1, call tokenize(pan, this). If it returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, return that marker straight up the stack. The thread is now free.
  2. When the vault answers, someone calls resumeWith(token). That calls chargeCard again with the same object. A tableswitch on label jumps to state 1, which picks up the token and calls authorize.
  3. Label 2: take the result and return it to whoever is waiting.

If tokenize does not suspend (a cache hit, say), it returns the token directly and the function carries on. Nothing is scheduled and no thread changes.

This explains both the cost and the rules. A suspended coroutine is one small object holding a label and a few fields, not a thread stack, so you can have hundreds of thousands. And plain code cannot call a suspend function, because it has no continuation to pass in.

sections.h: Wrapping a callback API with suspendCancellableCoroutine
sections.html:
Most vendor SDKs in payments take a callback or return a future. suspendCancellableCoroutine turns a callback into a suspend function. It suspends the coroutine and hands you its continuation, and you resume it when the callback fires.

Java
// Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback, and pass cancellation back
CompletableFuture<Integer> scoreAsync(Sdk sdk, String paymentId) {
    CompletableFuture<Integer> result = new CompletableFuture<>();
    Runnable cancel = sdk.score(paymentId, result::complete);          // 1. start; complete on callback
    result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); });   // 2. timed out or cancelled: tell the SDK
    return result;
}
Kotlin
suspend fun FraudSdk.scoreAwait(paymentId: String): Int =
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        val cancel = score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) }   // 1. start; resume on callback
        cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }                   // 2. we were cancelled: tell the SDK
    }

Three rules make a wrapper like this correct.

Resume exactly once. Call resume with a value or resumeWithException with an error. A second resume on the same continuation throws IllegalStateException.

Use the cancellable version. The standard library also has suspendCoroutine, and it works fine until someone cancels the caller. Then it can't react. The coroutine stays suspended until the SDK calls back, so a timeout fires late, and the SDK never hears that you gave up. In the Try it, a 100 ms timeout returns after a full second.

Expect late replies. If the coroutine is cancelled first, a callback that arrives afterwards is ignored. kotlinx.coroutines calls this the prompt cancellation guarantee: a cancelled coroutine does not resume successfully, even if the value was already on its way. If that late value is a resource, such as a pooled session, pass a cleanup lambda: cont.resume(session) { _, late, _ -> late.close() }. The library calls it when the value can no longer be delivered.

This tool is for callbacks that fire once. For listeners that fire many times you want callbackFlow (lesson 9 of this track). For a CompletableFuture you don't write any of this: future.await() in kotlinx-coroutines-core already does it (lesson 11 of this track).

try.title: Make a timeout reach the SDK
steps: Read CallbackBridge.kt. The SDK answers after one second. The caller allows 100 ms. Predict how long withTimeout(100) takes to return.
Run it.

Change scoreAwait to use suspendCancellableCoroutine (import kotlinx.coroutines.suspendCancellableCoroutine). Keep the function the SDK returns: val cancel = score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) }, then add cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }.
Run it again.
In the Java twin, run it, then add result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); }); before return result; and run it again.

code.title: CallbackBridge.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.coroutines.resume import kotlin.coroutines.suspendCoroutine import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** A fraud-scoring SDK with a callback API. It answers after 1 second on its own thread. */ class FraudSdk { private val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "fraud-sdk").apply { isDaemon = true } } fun score(paymentId: String, onScore: (Int) -> Unit): () -> Unit { val task = pool.schedule({ onScore(17) }, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) return { println(" sdk: request for $paymentId cancelled"); task.cancel(false) } } } // Wrapped with suspendCoroutine: works, but cancellation cannot reach it. suspend fun FraudSdk.scoreAwait(paymentId: String): Int = suspendCoroutine { cont -> score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val sdk = FraudSdk() val took = measureTimeMillis { try { withTimeout(100) { sdk.scoreAwait("pay_981") } } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { println(" timed out") } } println("withTimeout(100) returned after $took ms") }

alt.title: CallbackBridgeJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CallbackBridge.kt: wrap the callback SDK in a CompletableFuture. // The SDK answers after 1 second; the caller allows 100 ms. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; public class CallbackBridgeJava { /** A fraud-scoring SDK with a callback API. It answers after 1 second on its own thread. */ static final class Sdk { private final ScheduledExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "fraud-sdk"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); Runnable score(String paymentId, IntConsumer onScore) { ScheduledFuture<?> task = pool.schedule(() -> onScore.accept(17), 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); return () -> { System.out.println(" sdk: request for " + paymentId + " cancelled"); task.cancel(false); }; } } // Wrapped as a future: the caller can time out, but nothing tells the SDK yet. static CompletableFuture<Integer> scoreAsync(Sdk sdk, String paymentId) { CompletableFuture<Integer> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Runnable cancel = sdk.score(paymentId, result::complete); return result; } public static void main(String[] args) { Sdk sdk = new Sdk(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { scoreAsync(sdk, "pay_981").orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) System.out.println(" timed out"); } System.out.printf("orTimeout(100) returned after %d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); try { Thread.sleep(1_100); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } // was the SDK told? } }

try.expect: First run: timed out after about 1,000 ms (1,014 ms here). The timeout did fire at 100 ms, but suspendCoroutine could not wake up until the SDK answered, and the SDK was never told. After the change: sdk: request for pay_981 cancelled, then timed out after about 100 ms (116 ms here). The Java twin returns at about 100 ms even before your change, because orTimeout completes the future by itself, but the SDK only hears about it once you add the whenComplete hook.

analogy: A continuation is a bookmark with a sticky note. When a cook (a thread) reaches a step that needs the oven for 40 minutes, they don't stand at the oven. They put a bookmark in the recipe, write on the note which step comes next and which ingredients are already measured, and go cook something else. When the oven timer rings, any free cook can pick up the book, read the note, and carry on from that step. The recipe is the state machine, the step number is label, and the measured ingredients are the L$ fields. The analogy breaks in one place: in a kitchen the free cook picks up the book on their own. In a coroutine, the dispatcher decides who picks it up, and the callback that rings the timer is the only thing that can wake it.
world: Your services talk to an issuer SDK, an HSM client, a fraud-scoring vendor and a tokenization vault. Several of them hand you a callback or a future. Wrap each one once, with suspendCancellableCoroutine or future.await(), and the rest of the code base gets plain sequential functions with normal try/catch. More important for payments: when the caller's timeout fires, the cancel reaches the vendor call, so you are not left with a charge in flight that nobody is waiting for. The same rule applies in a Kafka consumer or a Temporal activity written in Kotlin: a retry backoff written with Thread.sleep holds the thread and stalls every other coroutine scheduled on it. Use delay.
mistake: The common mistake is thinking suspend makes code non-blocking. People mark a function suspend, call JDBC or Thread.sleep inside it, and expect the thread to be free while it waits. It isn't. suspend only lets a function pause at suspending calls such as delay, await or a suspendCancellableCoroutine wrapper. A blocking call inside a suspend function still blocks the thread. Wait with delay, wrap callback APIs with suspendCancellableCoroutine, and move unavoidable blocking calls to Dispatchers.IO with withContext (lesson 4 of this track).

compare.title: Two calls in a row: CompletableFuture vs suspend

java.title: ChargeService.java
java.html: CompletableFuture<String> chargeCard(String pan) { return vault.tokenize(pan) // CompletableFuture<String> .thenCompose(token -> issuer.authorize(token)) // CompletableFuture<String> .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); }

kotlin.title: ChargeService.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun chargeCard(pan: String): String = withTimeout(2.seconds) { val token = vault.tokenize(pan) // suspend fun issuer.authorize(token) // suspend fun }

compare.note: Both versions free the thread while they wait. The Java version expresses "then" with callbacks: each thenCompose registers a lambda, errors arrive wrapped in CompletionException, and orTimeout only completes the outer future exceptionally. The vault and issuer calls keep running, because cancelling a CompletableFuture never interrupts the work behind it. The Kotlin version reads like blocking code: locals, try/catch and loops all work, and the compiler builds the callbacks for you. When withTimeout fires, it cancels the coroutine, and cancellation reaches the two calls if they are written to cooperate, as in section 4. On JDK 21+ you can also write the Java version as plain blocking calls on a virtual thread. Lesson 11 of this track has a guide for choosing between the two.

worked.title: Wrap a pooled-session SDK without leaking sessions

steps.say: An HSM vendor hands out sessions from a pool. acquire returns at once with a Ticket and calls you back later with a session or an error. Sessions must be closed. You want suspend fun HsmPool.acquireAwait(): Session.
steps.code: class Session(val id: Int) : AutoCloseable { override fun close() { /* back to the pool */ } } fun interface Ticket { fun cancel() } interface HsmPool { fun acquire(onReady: (Session?, Throwable?) -> Unit): Ticket }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same SDK shape final class Session implements AutoCloseable { @Override public void close() { /* back to the pool */ } } interface Ticket { void cancel(); } interface HsmPool { Ticket acquire(BiConsumer<Session, Throwable> onReady); }

steps.say: Start the request inside suspendCancellableCoroutine and resume exactly once from the callback: a value on success, an exception on error.
steps.code: suspend fun HsmPool.acquireAwait(): Session = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> // 1. start the request; the pool calls back on its own thread val ticket = acquire { session, error -> // 2. resume exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) cont.resumeWithException(error) else cont.resume(session!!) } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback static CompletableFuture<Session> acquireAsync(HsmPool pool) { CompletableFuture<Session> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); // 1. start the request; the pool calls back on its own thread Ticket ticket = pool.acquire((session, error) -> { // 2. complete exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) result.completeExceptionally(error); else result.complete(session); }); return result; }

steps.say: If the caller times out, stop waiting for a session. invokeOnCancellation runs when the coroutine is cancelled while suspended here.
steps.code: // 3. our caller gave up: cancel the ticket cont.invokeOnCancellation { ticket.cancel() }

alt.html: // 3. our caller gave up (cancelled the future): cancel the ticket result.whenComplete((s, e) -> { if (result.isCancelled()) ticket.cancel(); });

steps.say: One gap is left. The pool may hand out a session just after you were cancelled. The continuation ignores that late resume, and the session leaks. Use the resume overload that takes a cleanup lambda: the library calls it with the value it could not deliver.
steps.code: else cont.resume(session!!) { _, late, _ -> late.close() } // 4. late session: close it

alt.html: // 4. late session: complete() returns false when the future is already done, so close it else if (!result.complete(session)) session.close();

steps.say: Self-check: why is step 4 needed even though step 3 cancels the ticket? (Cancelling is a request. The pool may already be calling you back on another thread, so the session can still arrive after you were cancelled.)

lab.title: Wrap the issuer SDK, then fix a blocking backoff
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail: four hit the TODO in authorizeAwait, and the backoff test shows the coroutines running one after another.
Read IssuerSdk.kt. It is the vendor's callback API; do not change it.
Write authorizeAwait in SuspendingIssuer.kt with suspendCancellableCoroutine. Start the request with an AuthCallback object whose two methods resume the continuation.
Register invokeOnCancellation so that a cancelled caller calls cancel() on the InFlight handle.

Run the tests until all five pass.
hints: An anonymous object implements the callback: object : AuthCallback { override fun onApproved(auth: Authorization) = cont.resume(auth); ... }.
If the cancellation test hangs for 10 seconds, you used suspendCoroutine. It cannot react to cancellation, so cancelAndJoin waits forever.
The backoff test runs under runTest, which skips delay on virtual time. That is why it expects currentTime to be exactly 200.

drill.title: Wrap a callback from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A BIN lookup SDK has fun lookup(bin: String, cb: (BinInfo?, Throwable?) -> Unit): Call, and Call has a cancel() method. Write suspend fun BinSdk.lookupAwait(bin: String): BinInfo so that errors are thrown and a cancelled caller cancels the call. Then compare.

answer.html: suspend fun BinSdk.lookupAwait(bin: String): BinInfo = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> val call = lookup(bin) { info, error -> if (error != null) cont.resumeWithException(error) else cont.resume(info!!) } cont.invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a CompletableFuture that cancels the call when it is cancelled static CompletableFuture<BinInfo> lookupAsync(BinSdk sdk, String bin) { CompletableFuture<BinInfo> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Call call = sdk.lookup(bin, (info, error) -> { if (error != null) result.completeExceptionally(error); else result.complete(info); }); result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (result.isCancelled()) call.cancel(); }); return result; }

recap: suspend lets a function pause at suspending calls without holding a thread. It does not choose a thread or run anything in the background.
delay suspends and frees the thread; Thread.sleep blocks it, and every coroutine that needs that thread waits.
The compiler adds a Continuation parameter, returns Any? (COROUTINE_SUSPENDED or the result), and turns the body into a state machine with a label and fields for live locals.
A coroutine may resume on a different thread after a suspension, so ThreadLocal values don't follow it, but your own writes stay visible.
Wrap single-shot callbacks with suspendCancellableCoroutine: resume exactly once, cancel the underlying call in invokeOnCancellation, and expect late replies.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "I marked our ledger lookup suspend, so it no longer blocks the request thread." The lookup uses plain JDBC inside. Explain what suspend actually changed, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: suspend only gives the function the ability to pause at suspending calls, and the compiler adds a continuation parameter so it can be resumed later. It does not move the code to another thread. A JDBC call is blocking, not suspending, so the function never pauses: it holds the request thread for the whole query, exactly as before. To keep the request thread free, the blocking call has to run somewhere else, for example withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { jdbc... }, or the driver has to offer a suspending or async API that we wrap with suspendCancellableCoroutine or await().

deeper.html:
Kotlin coroutines and Java virtual threads both rest on continuations, but they put them in different places.

Kotlin's continuations are stackless. The compiler rewrites each suspend function into a state machine, and a suspended coroutine is a chain of those small state objects, one per suspend function still in progress. That is why suspend is part of the function type: every function between the coroutine and the suspending call must be compiled this way, or there is nowhere to save its state. People call this function coloring. It is also why coroutines work on any JVM version, on Android, and on Kotlin/JS and Native, where there is no Loom.

Virtual threads use stackful continuations inside the JVM. When a virtual thread blocks, the JVM copies its stack frames to the heap and unmounts it from the carrier. Any blocking call, in any library, can pause it, with no change to the code and no coloring. The price is that the JVM decides when to pause, and code that holds a monitor or calls native code could pin the carrier on older JDKs (JDK 24 removed most pinning on synchronized, JEP 491).

The KEEP also explains a detail you saw in javap: the state object is created once per call and reused across every suspension point in that call, so a function that suspends three times allocates one object, not three. And a suspend function whose suspending calls are all in tail position needs no state machine at all; it passes its continuation straight through.

Read the "Implementation details" part of the KEEP (linked in sources) if you want the pseudo-Java the compiler generates, including how the generated invokeSuspend method re-enters the function.
